content: Cardiovascular technologists and technicians play a critical role in assisting physicians with the diagnosis and treatment of heart and blood vessel conditions. These professionals may specialize in one of three main areas: invasive cardiology, echocardiography, or vascular technology. Cardiovascular technicians who focus on electrocardiograms (EKGs), stress testing, and Holter monitoring are referred to as cardiographic or EKG technicians. Those specializing in invasive procedures are known as invasive cardiovascular technologists. These technologists assist physicians during cardiac catheterization procedures, where a catheter is inserted into a patient’s artery, typically starting at the groin, and guided to the heart. This procedure helps identify blockages in the blood vessels supplying the heart and can also diagnose other cardiac issues. In some cases, balloon angioplasty is performed during the procedure to treat blockages in blood vessels or heart valves without requiring open-heart surgery. In such cases, invasive cardiovascular technologists assist in guiding a catheter with a balloon to the site of the obstruction. Before cardiac catheterization or balloon angioplasty, invasive cardiovascular technologists prepare the patient by positioning them on the examination table, shaving and cleaning the area near the groin, and administering local anesthesia. These technologists may also assist during open-heart surgeries and the placement of pacemakers or stents, which are used to open blocked arteries in the heart or major blood vessels. Cardiac sonographers, another type of cardiovascular technologist, use ultrasound equipment to examine the heart’s chambers, valves, and blood vessels. They produce images called echocardiograms, which can be performed while the patient is at rest or during physical activity. In some cases, cardiac sonographers administer medications to patients during physical activity to evaluate heart function. They may also assist physicians in performing transesophageal echocardiography, a procedure where a tube is inserted into the patient’s esophagus to obtain detailed ultrasound images of the heart. Vascular technologists, also known as vascular specialists or vascular sonographers, assist in diagnosing disorders affecting blood circulation. They begin by taking a patient’s medical history, evaluating pulses, and listening to blood flow sounds for abnormalities. Many of these tests are conducted during or immediately after surgery. Electrocardiograph (EKG) technicians are responsible for obtaining basic EKG readings, which trace the electrical impulses of the heart. To perform an EKG, they attach electrodes to the patient’s chest, arms, and legs and operate the EKG machine to produce a reading. The results are printed for interpretation by a physician. EKGs are commonly performed before surgeries or as part of routine physical exams, particularly for middle-aged individuals or those with a history of heart problems. EKG technicians with advanced training may also perform Holter monitoring and stress testing. For Holter monitoring, they attach electrodes to the patient’s chest and connect a portable EKG monitor to the patient’s belt. After 24 or more hours of normal activity, the technician retrieves the monitor, scans the recorded data, and prints the results for physician analysis. This test helps diagnose heart rhythm abnormalities or issues with pacemakers. They then monitor the heart’s performance as the patient walks on a treadmill, gradually increasing the speed to observe the heart’s response to physical exertion. Cardiographic technicians, vascular technologists, and cardiac sonographers who perform noninvasive procedures such as EKGs, Holter monitoring, and stress tests are collectively referred to as “noninvasive” technicians.
